## Key Takeaways:


---


- Integrating multiple biometric markers helps agencies connect people to records, scenes and cases with greater confidence.
- Connecting local evidence with national systems can reveal cross-jurisdictional links and patterns across cases.
- Super Intelligence (SI) brings AI-enabled identity intelligence together with human insight to help accelerate investigations into fraud, trafficking and other complex crimes.


---


Biometric and identity data are the thread that ties together otherwise siloed records, systems and jurisdictions. On their own, a name in a database, a ballistics image on a single cartridge case, a face on a camera and even a print at a violent crime scene are merely fragments. Linked, they could help establish probable cause. When an agency can reliably identify and differentiate persons of interest across multi-source platforms, fragmented information begins to function like a connected, mission-driven ecosystem.


## Recognition Is the Starting Point


Law enforcement already uses facial recognition to help identify suspects, pursue leads and locate missing persons. However, facial recognition is only the most widely known technology in a rapidly growing list of tools.


Modern identity intelligence draws on a range of biometric markers, each useful in different conditions. These include voice recognition, iris scans that capture a unique pattern, retinal scans that read blood-vessel structure, hand geometry, keystroke dynamics that reveal typing patterns and even gait analysis that identifies a person by how they move. No single marker is a silver bullet. Their value lies in combination. The more signals an agency can integrate, the more confidently it can connect a person to a record, scene or case.


Facial recognition technology continues to improve, and synthetic data is giving developers another way to strengthen how algorithms are trained and tested. Rather than relying solely on real-world images, developers can generate synthetic images that represent a wider range of faces, characteristics and conditions. Used appropriately, these datasets can help fill gaps in real-world training data and improve how algorithms perform across different populations and operating environments. But the quality and diversity of the synthetic data matter. If not carefully designed and tested, synthetic data can reinforce existing biases rather than reduce them.


## Connection in Action: The Crime Scene


The crime scene provides one of the strongest examples of identity as a connective thread, with several systems working together to deliver better solvability-based outcomes.


AI can help assess a scene, especially when drawing on trusted, real-time data from fusion centers, crime gun intelligence centers or records management systems. It can support 3D scene reconstruction from images and video, enhance surveillance footage, and assist with ballistics, blood spatter and DNA analysis.


The value increases when analysis extends beyond local systems to national resources such as the National Integrated Ballistic Information Network (NIBIN) for ballistics and the Combined DNA Index System (CODIS) for DNA.


##### The identity is the link; the connection is what transforms it into intelligence.


Ballistics and DNA may lead nowhere inside a single jurisdiction. When connected to national systems and real-time, intelligence-driven data streams, that same evidence could tie a scene to a suspect, a suspect to a pattern, and a pattern to one or more cases that have long gone cold.


The identity is the link; the connection is what transforms it into intelligence. For the safety of our communities and the success of our public safety professionals, that connectivity matters.


## Beyond the Crime Scene


Identity intelligence has value beyond physical evidence. AI algorithms can also monitor transactions in real time. Using behavioral biometrics, or the subtle patterns in how a legitimate user behaves, AI can flag anomalies that signal identity theft or fraud. The same capabilities can be used to verify identity documents, detect and thwart phishing attempts, and monitor for the signals that precede a range of financial crimes.


AI-enabled capabilities are already supporting faster response and investigative work across challenges like narcotics trafficking, human trafficking and money laundering. These are precisely the kinds of cross-jurisdictional crimes that fragmented identity data cannot follow. That is the promise of identity as a connective thread. When the fragments come together, the mission can move faster than the threat.


Connecting data across systems and agencies raises critical questions about how to make these connections while keeping data secure. That is the topic we explore in our next installment.
